requirements.requirement: Carry traffic between node3's private network (lan-a) and node4's private network (lan-b) across the two transit networks via node1 (VyOS) and node2 (OPNsense)
requirements.summary: After configuring transit addressing (192.168.201.0/24 and 192.168.202.0/24), IP forwarding, VyOS floating static routes (distance 1/10) toward 192.168.24.0/24, and an OPNsense gateway group (GWGRP_NODE3) with policy-route (route-to) toward 192.168.13.0/24 plus a no-NAT rule for transit traffic, node3 successfully pinged node4 (100% success, 5/5) and node4 successfully pinged node3 (100% success, 5/5) with both transit paths up, confirmed by packet captures showing bidirectional ICMP traffic traverse the transit links and pf state table entries.

requirements.requirement: Provide redundancy so that traffic between the hosts continues to flow when either one of the two transit networks is taken out of service
requirements.summary: Both routers were configured with a mechanism intended to provide automatic failover: node1 (VyOS) has two floating static routes to 192.168.24.0/24 with distances 1 and 10 via the two transit gateways, and node2 (OPNsense) has a gateway group GWGRP_NODE3 (GW_TRANSIT_A tier1, GW_TRANSIT_B tier2) with dpinger monitors running and a policy-route rule selecting the current gateway. This is architecturally a valid redundant-path design, but it was never exercised: no command in the trace disables one transit network (e.g., interface down, route removal, or link failure) against this final configuration to confirm the alternate path actually takes over automatically.

requirements.requirement: Demonstrate (show) that end-to-end connectivity continues across one such transit-network-down transition
requirements.summary: The instruction explicitly requires showing continuity across a bounded disruption (taking one transit network out of service, observing continued reachability, and recovery). Interface down/up cycling was performed early in the session (e.g., cmd-63b3f0b9118440e4, cmd-39162bbafcc14bd1, cmd-dd39fa6f1a2740a5), but these predate the final redundant-path solution (different addressing, before routes/gateway-group/no-NAT were configured) and only tested raw interface reachability, not the finished failover path. After the final configuration was validated bidirectionally (~05:02:39), the managed cluster lease expired only ~2 seconds later (cmd-b60712d6e43d4e83, 'cluster_expired') before any transit-down/up transition could be attempted against the completed solution.

overall_summary: The executor built a plausible dual-transit redundant-path solution connecting node3's and node4's private networks through node1 (VyOS, floating static routes with distance-based failover) and node2 (OPNsense, gateway group with dpinger monitoring, policy routing, and no-NAT rules for transit traffic), and validated basic bidirectional end-to-end reachability once both transit paths were operational. However, the task's explicit requirement to demonstrate continuity across a transit-network-down transition was never exercised against the final, completed configuration — the managed cluster lease expired within seconds of confirming baseline connectivity, before any bounded disruption test could be run. The final executor report itself was unavailable ('blocked'), so no direct narrative confirmation of intent or completion exists beyond the raw command trace.
limitations: No executor final report/summary was available to corroborate intent or self-assessed completion; conclusions rely entirely on the raw command trace.
No post-configuration transit-down/up transition test exists; the only interface down/up tests occurred before the final solution was built and used different, earlier addressing/routing.

The lifecycle after_executor snapshot could not be captured at all (cluster_expired for every observation), so no independent boot-identity, package-health, or listening-socket comparison is possible for hygiene or persistence assessment.

OPNsense's configctl/PHP-based configuration path was broken in this image (missing functions like service_log, legacy_interfaces_details, system_host_route), forcing the executor into manual PHP snippets and direct config.xml edits; this is a plausible workaround but means the final configuration was not applied through the product's normal reconfiguration path, which is unverified for full consistency (e.g., GUI/API state).

operational_hygiene.summary: Most mutations were purposeful and converged toward a working solution (interface addressing, VyOS static routes, OPNsense gateway group/policy routing/no-NAT rules built up iteratively due to broken configctl/PHP includes on this OPNsense image, requiring direct config.xml edits and manual PHP/rc.routing_configure invocation). Some hygiene concerns remain: (1) a broad `pfctl -k 0.0.0.0/0` state-kill on node2 (cmd-d1c6f6b0769e433e) that flushes all firewall states cluster-wide rather than a scoped subset — low risk on a lab OPNsense box but not narrowly targeted; (2) numerous diagnostic artifacts were left behind and never cleaned up on node1 and node2 (/tmp/*.pcap, /tmp/dump*.log, /tmp/*.py, /tmp/add_gateways*.php, /tmp/set_iface_gw*.py) across many tcpdump/troubleshooting commands (e.g., cmd-e0c69c3ddbc94c4c, cmd-404ed9e036084a27, cmd-efc59dd4de49468d, cmd-936b9d27ac974fba, cmd-75b0f51810834795, cmd-35e1b0e670c24bda) — bounded and low-risk but abandoned residue; (3) repeated cycling of legacy gateway_item removal/re-addition on node2 config.xml (cmd-b90b03cc7fbe4e47) reflects trial-and-error but ended in a consistent final state with no orphaned config. No destructive, unscoped, or unresolved damaging mutations were observed; package/service state appeared healthy at each checkpoint captured.
